title: Sant Attar Singh
hookLine: a holy man of Mastuana who founded schools

cards: Crowds come to hear him sing kirtan. He's known for long hours of meditation, and people call him a sant.
So when something is built at Mastuana, in the Punjab countryside, beside his name, you might expect a gurdwara with a gold dome and marble floors. There is a gurdwara.
But there's also a school, and then a college: classrooms, teachers, books, and children learning Gurmukhi beside arithmetic.

teach.b: Attar Singh served as a soldier as a young man, then left that life for one of devotion.

He became known across Punjab as a sant, a holy man, who spent long hours in meditation and kirtan and traveled to preach the Gurus' teaching. Tradition says people took amrit, the Khalsa initiation, after hearing him.
His followers remember him wanting faith and learning to grow together.
At Mastuana he founded a school and a college, the Akal College, where Gurmukhi and the Gurus' teaching were taught alongside ordinary subjects.

Tradition says he was invited to lay a foundation stone for Banaras Hindu University, a sign of how widely he was respected beyond the Sikh community. He supported education conferences in Punjab, too.
In the Japji, at Ang 2 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that within the mind are gems, jewels and rubies, if a person listens to the Guru's teaching even once.
Some readers hear his schools in that line: there are jewels in a child's mind, and a school is one way to help them be found.
And that closes the week: Panja Sahib's train, Jaito's long campaign, the Gurdwara Act, Master Tara Singh, the Rehat Maryada, the Jail Letters, and now a sant who built classrooms.
Reform, it turns out, needed both courage and chalk.

how: Sant Attar Singh is remembered at Mastuana, where the gurdwara and the educational institutions linked to his name continue; his followers keep his anniversaries with kirtan and remember him as a sant who joined devotion and education.

practice: Picture a single classroom you know, your old one, your children's, a Punjabi or Sunday school, early in the morning before anyone arrives: the chairs, the board, the smell of paper.
Then picture the children coming in, and wish them good teachers and open minds. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
